direct_page_evidence.text:
21
VISUAL DISORDERS (I)
Vision plays an important role in driving and safety.  The guidelines require you to have 20/40 vision  
in at least one eye and a visual field of at least 90° to drive a Class D (regular) vehicle.  When visiting 
a field office or if you are older than 65 at the time of your driver license application, you will be re-
quired to pass a vision test.
If unable to pass a vision test you will be requested to take a Certificate of Visual Examination form 
(CVE) to an ophthalmologist.  A completed vision form (CVE) should indicate your visual acuity and 
must be presented before your application for a license can be accepted.
MENTAL HEALTH (G)
Mental health conditions are as important as physical health.  If your mind is not on your driving, you 
are probably not driving safely.  The way we act and treat others can provide hints about our mental 
health:
• Always mad at other drivers and sometimes try to “get even.”
• Excessively confused or frustrated when traffic becomes heavy.
• Depressed and worried about things that your attention is not always on the road.
• Frequently getting traffic citations.
• Having trouble adjusting to an emotional shock such as the loss of a loved one.
Tip 1: Give yourself time to cool off.  Take a walk or talk to a friend.  Do anything, but stay off the road 
until you have cooled down.
 
Tip 2: Do something that will allow you to concentrate on driving.  Listen to the radio or sing to your-
self.
Tip 3: Give yourself extra time.  Leave a few minutes early, you will not feel the need to speed, beat 
traffic signals, or anything that will result in a citation or a traffic accident.
ALCOHOL AND OTHER DRUGS (H)
Many medications may cause drowsiness or other difficulties; therefore, a physician may advise 
against driving until a suitable dosage schedule has been worked out that will not impair driving.  
Abuse or excessive use of prescription drugs has caused many serious accidents and should be 
avoided.
B. MEDICAL FORMS
You will be asked to answer health-related questions when applying for your Utah driver license.  If 
there is a health condition that may affect your driving, we will send you a Functional Ability Evalua-
tion (FAE) form by mail to take to your HCP.
An HCP is responsible for accurately completing the form, reporting your functional ability.
The completed form is returned to the Driver License Division for review.  If appropriate, a license to 
drive will be issued based on previously determined levels of driving risk and may result in license 
restrictions, skill and written knowledge testing (driver review) and in some cases, a denial of your 
license for safety reasons.  For example, if there is a vision condition and you cannot read highway 
signs at a distance, you may be considered unsafe to drive, and a restricted license would be issued.

22
You have the final responsibility for knowing your abilities and for driving safely.
C. REVIEW EXAMINATION (Driver Review)
Sometimes, the division will request a driver appear for a review examination.  The request for an 
evaluation may be based upon:
• A request from a medical professional.
• A confidential reporting.
• A law enforcement officer who observed a driving situation and questioned the driver’s ability 
to operate a motor vehicle safely.
• An individual or agency indicating a driver may be impaired.
• A returned FAE form recommending a review based on the medical guidelines.
A review examination does not necessarily lead to withdrawing the driving privilege.  In most cases, 
upon completion of the review process, a driver is allowed to drive under applicable restrictions if 
deemed safe by the division.  
Driving privileges are withdrawn if an individual does not complete a required review examination.
After the review examination is completed, a hearing officer discusses the results with the driver and 
reviews the medical evaluation (FAE).  The hearing officer takes into account:
• The driving needs of the individual.
• The type of roads or highways used.
• The traffic conditions usually experienced, etc.  
The hearing officer relies on the guidelines established by the Driver License Medical Advisory Board 
(MAB) as they relate to the medical form provided by the driver.  The hearing officer then decides 
whether any restrictions need to be placed on the license.  Often no restrictions are required, but 
when they are, one or more restrictions are specified on the license.
Only when the division determines a driver cannot operate a vehicle safely under any conditions are 
driving privileges withdrawn.
